#abrahamlincoln 
April 1865.
This long telegram is Lincoln's  response to Major-General Weitzel concerning Judge Campbell's (misspelled or encoded in the telegram as "Camel")  letter to the Major-General  concerning the legitimacy of the Virginia Legislature  to resolve their differences with the US.  Lincoln writes, "I deal with them as men having power de facto to do a specific thing, to wit: "To withdraw the Virginia troops and other support from resistance to the General Government" ... "and particularly as General Grant has since captured the Virginia troops, so that giving a consideration for their withdrawal is no longer applicable, let my letter to you and the paper to Judge Campbell both be withdrawn, or countermanded, and he be notified of it. Do not now allow them to assemble, but if any have come, allow them safe return to their homes."

http://www.civilwar-online.com/2015/04/april-12-1865-lincoln-revokes.html

In this amazing telegram, the second one on the page, sent two days after Lincoln's assassination on April 17, 1865, Gen William Tecumseh Sherman reveals that he has negotiated his own peace agreement with CSA Genl Johnston, disregarding the fact that such negotiations are for the politicians, not the military.   This without guidance from Washington.  This event was called the Sherman-Johnston Peace Agreement which would not reach Washington until April 21 and Secretary of War Stanton, President Johnson and all of Washington were apoplectic when they realized what he had done.   

See a version of the reaction in Washington in the free e-book Lincoln in the Telegraph Office p 395

https://play.google.com/books/reader?id=HyF3AAAAMAAJ&printsec=frontcover&output=reader&hl=en&pg=GBS.PA395

The author, one of the telegraph operators of the War Department, tells that he was required to take down Secy Stanton's response and Stanton was going so fast he couldn't keep up at which time Stanton erupted in anger.  Stanton later apologized and says he was so angry at Sherman he couldn't control himself.  The telegrapher, author David Homer Bates, described the agreement as follows:

"This was in connection with the sensational Sherman-Johnston Peace Agreement which reached Washington on April 21, 1865 (only 6 days after Lincoln's death), the contents of which were of such an extraordinary character as to cause Stanton to become intensely excited. In fact, every high official of the Government, not excluding General Grant, was amazed at Sheman's action in signing such an agreement. Major A. E. H. Johnson has told me that on one occasion, when he was discussing the subject, said that President Johnson at the historical conference on the evening of April 21, in Representative Hooper's house, after hearing Stanton read over his "Nine Reasons why the Sherman-Johnston Agreement Agreement should be rejected by the Government" remarked that Sherman was a traitor."

It appears in the telegram of April 17th that Sherman is clueless and actually giddy at his accomlishment.

"No more unapproved press dispatches"!  There follows two wildly differing accounts of the same battle and a third account found in "a bottle picked up May 20 off Hatteras" (if I understand correctly).  Whew!

General Rosecrans pleads to Gen. Halleck for more cavalry horses: "I have been urgent in asking for horses since October last. We have thirty five hundred dismounted Cavalry. If horses cannot be purchased they should be pressed."

#troopstrength 

Complains about being massively outnumbered; The enemy cavalry 4000 strong with fresh horses, and the union has three hundred and twenty men with sick and lame horses.

**Richmond Daily Dispatch**
       July 31, 1862
Another brilliant cavalry fight in Western Virginia.
A Town and its garrison captured.
Large quantities of the enemy stores destroyed.
Lynchburg, July 30.
--A special dispatch to the Republican, dated Narrows of New River,July 28th, via Dublin, July 29th, says:

The gallant Major Bailey commanding four companies of cavalry, in all about one hundred and fifty men, sent to the rear of the enemy by Col. McCausland, stormed Summerville, the county seat of Nicholas, Fridaymorning at daylight, and killed and captured the entire garrison, including the Lieutenant Colonel commanding, named Starr, three other commissioned officers, and sixty-two non-commissioned officers and privates, killing a large number. A few prisoners were paroled. Not being able to bring away the large quantities of commissary, quartermaster and ordnance stores found at the place, Major Bailey committed them to the flames. Major B. brought to this place a large number of Enfield rifles, horses and mules. The prisoners arrived this morning at the Salt Sulphur Springs. The notorious renegade and spy, Dr. Wm. Rucker, is among the prisoners. The telegraph office was destroyed, and the Government operator captured. --This affair is regarded as the most brilliant exploit of the war in this section. Its successful execution spread the wildest consternation and dismay throughout the Yankee army in the neighborhood.  from: *http://www.wvculture.org/history/sesquicentennial/18620725.html*
